title: Roman doctors still admit true fixed assent that yields peace—and redefine leftover fear
source_text: XLVII. Et tamen dissidium istud obscurius redditur, si consideremus quae partes dissidentes, dum inter se disputant, hinc & inde proferunt. Quandoquidem omnes Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae hic admittant veri nominis certitudinem, quae consistit in vero determinato, & fixo assensu, qui excludit omnem fluctuationem, & haesitationem, nec animum dubium & suspensum relinquit: & tantam in homine fideli fiduciam, ut sufficiat ad pacem & tranquillitatem animi, & spirituale gaudium, & hominem securum reddat de Dei gratia: adeoque fatentur bonos fideles certissime credere se esse in gratia, nec se falli in hac sua opinione; & formidinem illam, quae cum ista fidelium persuasione consistit, aiunt in eo constituendam esse, quod boni isti fideles credunt quidem se in eo non falli, sed tamen non credunt se falli non posse; talem quippe certitudinem propriam esse solius fidei divinitus infusae.
pass_a_gloss: And yet that disagreement is rendered more obscure if we consider what the dissenting parties, while they dispute among themselves, bring forward from this side and that. Since indeed all the doctors of the Roman Church here admit a certainty of true name, which consists in a true determinate and fixed assent that excludes every fluctuation and hesitation and does not leave the mind doubtful and suspended; and so great a trust in the faithful person that it suffices for peace and tranquillity of soul and spiritual joy and renders the person secure concerning God’s grace: and so they confess that good faithful people most certainly believe that they are in grace and that they are not deceived in this their opinion; and that fear which consists with that persuasion of the faithful they say is to be constituted in this, that those good faithful believe indeed that they are not deceived in it, but nevertheless do not believe that they cannot be deceived; for such certainty is proper to infused divine faith alone.
pass_b_english: Rome grants fixed, peace-giving assent that one is in grace.
Their leftover ‘fear’ is meta-epistemic: I am not deceived—yet I do not believe deception is impossible.
